summary: Recommends improving OSPF Version 2 scalability and stability in large networks by processing Hello and LSA acknowledgment packets at higher priority and using congestion avoidance procedures. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: In a traffic jam, the doorbell should still ring. This memo says routers should answer important OSPF messages first so big networks stay stable.

questions: what is an ospf lsa storm
how to limit simultaneous ospf adjacencies
subtitle: How OSPF routers can keep Hellos and acknowledgments flowing during an LSA storm so large networks stay up.

tldr.problem: When a large OSPF network floods a burst of link state advertisements, routers can delay Hellos and acknowledgments, causing retransmissions and false adjacency failures that feed on themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends handling Hello and LSA Acknowledgment packets ahead of other OSPF packets, backing off LSA retransmissions and sending rates exponentially, and limiting how many adjacencies are brought up at once.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice. The metadata shows it is updated by RFC 9454, so read that RFC alongside it.

today: RFC 4222 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 112), and the unit metadata lists it as updated by RFC 9454. Read that RFC together with this one.

sections.title: LSA Storms and Why They Hurt
sections.content:
This RFC is about OSPF Version 2. A large network can occasionally see many link state advertisements (LSAs) updated at nearly the same time. The RFC calls this an LSA storm. It can start from a failure or a scheduled maintenance event, and it is more likely when the OSPF traffic engineering extension is used because that can greatly increase the number of LSAs.

The storm causes high CPU and memory use at routers, so incoming packets are delayed or dropped. Delayed acknowledgments lead to retransmissions. Delayed Hello packets, beyond the router-dead interval, lead to neighbor adjacencies being declared down. The extra retransmissions and LSA originations use more CPU and memory, a positive feedback loop that in the extreme may drive the network into an unstable state.

The default retransmission timer is 5 seconds and the default router-dead interval is 40 seconds. Proposals for much shorter, sub-second Hello and router-dead intervals make late Hellos during congestion more likely.
sections.eli5: If too many messages arrive at once, a router gets so busy that it forgets to say hello to its neighbors. The neighbors think it has gone away, and that creates even more messages.

sections.title: Prioritizing Hellos and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
Recommendation 1 splits OSPF packets into two classes by looking at the OSPF packet header. The high priority class is Hello packets and Link State Acknowledgment packets. Everything else is low priority. A router should try to process a high priority packet ahead of a low priority one, both when receiving from a neighbor and when transmitting to one.

There is a catch with Cryptographic Authentication (AuType = 2). Reordering at the transmitter can make packets arrive out of sequence, but received packets need non-decreasing cryptographic sequence numbers. So with cryptographic authentication, the RFC recommends not prioritizing at the transmitter. Prioritizing at the receiver, after security processing and sequence number checking, is still beneficial.

Recommendation 2 is a fallback for routers that cannot do Recommendation 1. It resets the inactivity timer when any OSPF unicast packet, or any packet sent to AllSPFRouters over a point-to-point link, arrives on an adjacency, instead of only on a Hello. The RFC says not to combine it with Recommendation 1, because stale packets in the low priority queue could keep resetting the timer and delay discovery that an adjacency is down.
sections.eli5: Imagine two mail slots, one for urgent notes like are you still there and got it, and one for everything else. The router reads the urgent slot first.

sections.title: Backing Off Under Congestion
sections.content:
Recommendation 3 applies exponential backoff to the LSA retransmission interval. With R(1) = Rmin and R(i+1) = Min(K*R(i), Rmax), each retransmission of the same LSA waits longer, up to a cap. Example values are K = 2, Rmin = 5 seconds and Rmax = 40 seconds. Repeated retransmissions are a major source of sustained congestion, so slowing them helps the network recover.

Recommendation 4 lets a router detect a congested neighbor implicitly, from the number of unacknowledged LSAs sent to it. If that number exceeds a high-water mark H, the gap between successive LSAs to that neighbor grows by a factor F, up to Gmax. If it falls below a low-water mark L, the gap shrinks by F, down to Gmin. The gap is only reconsidered after a time T has passed. It is applied independently to each neighbor, and only for unicast LSAs or LSAs sent to AllSPFRouters over a point-to-point link.

The RFC contrasts the two: Recommendation 3 slows successive retransmissions of the same LSA, while Recommendation 4 slows all LSAs, new or retransmitted, to a congested neighbor.
sections.eli5: If a friend keeps not answering, you wait a bit longer each time before asking again, and you send fewer notes at once. When they start answering, you speed back up.

sections.title: Throttling New Adjacencies
sections.content:
Recommendation 5 addresses a router that tries to bring up many adjacencies at once. Database synchronization and LSA flooding for all of them can cause severe congestion. The RFC recommends that no more than n adjacencies be brought up simultaneously, with new ones started as earlier ones finish. The value of n should be configurable and depends on router processing power, control plane bandwidth and propagation delay.

For ordering, a First Come First Served policy is recommended, based on when requests arrive from neighbors or are self-generated. Among self-generated requests, a priority list may be used. Once an adjacency starts forming, it is not preempted except for unusual circumstances such as errors or time-outs.

The RFC also says references to point-to-point links in these recommendations should include cases where a broadcast network is treated as a point-to-point connection for IP routing.
sections.eli5: If a teacher meets thirty new students, she talks to a few at a time rather than all at once, so nobody gets lost in the crowd.

sections.title: Example Parameter Values
sections.content:
Appendix B lists the variables used above with example values. They are examples, not mandated settings. The RFC gives F = 2, K = 2, H = 20, L = 10, T = 1 second, Gmin = 20 ms, Gmax = 1 second, Rmin = 5 seconds and Rmax = 40 seconds. The limit n on simultaneous adjacencies has no example value.

Appendix A adds background. It lists causes of LSA storms, such as fiber cuts, router failures, link flapping, upgrades, near-synchronized 1800-second LSA refreshes and procedural errors that inject many external routes. It describes a simulation study that found a storm size threshold above which a network may turn unstable, and reports that prioritizing Hello and acknowledgment packets and using exponential backoff for retransmissions increased the storm size the network could withstand.
sections.eli5: The memo gives sample settings, like how many unanswered notes are too many, but each network can pick its own numbers.

sections.title: Extra Suggestions
sections.content:
Appendix C offers optional ideas. Explicit marking uses different TOS or Precedence values for high and low priority packets so a router need not parse the OSPF header. OSPF normally uses TOS 0 and Precedence 6. One example sets high priority packets to TOS 4 and Precedence 6, another to TOS 0 and Precedence 7. The RFC notes these bits were redefined by Diffserv in RFC 2474.

The RFC also suggests a three-class scheme with a medium priority, for example a Database Description packet from a slave used as an acknowledgment, or an LSA carrying intra-area topology change. Finally, it considers processing LSA purges ahead of originations but does not recommend out-of-order LSA processing, citing computational cost and the risk of subtle bugs.
sections.eli5: You can also put a colored sticker on urgent mail so the sorter does not need to open each envelope to tell which is urgent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that this memo does not create any new security issues for the OSPF protocol. The only security-related guidance in the recommendations concerns cryptographic authentication: prioritizing at the transmitter is avoided so that packets do not break the sequence number requirement of AuType = 2.
sections.eli5: The memo does not open any new doors for troublemakers. It just takes care not to break the existing lock.

viz.caption: RETRANSMISSION BACKOFF AND SENDING GAP (RFC 4222, RECOMMENDATIONS 3 AND 4)

data.title: Backoff formulas
data.code:
R(1) = Rmin
R(i+1) = Min(K*R(i), Rmax)   for i>=1

G(t+T) = Min(F*G(t), Gmax)   if U(t+T) > H
G(t+T) = G(t)                if H >= U(t+T) >= L
G(t+T) = Max(G(t)/F, Gmin)   if U(t+T) < L
